flawed_step: Step 5: Three attachment vertices on a cycle need not include two consecutive vertices; they may be separated around the cycle.
counterexample: The Petersen graph, realized as the graph whose vertices are the 2-element subsets of {1,2,3,4,5}, with adjacency defined by disjointness, is finite, simple, 3-regular, 3-connected, and non-Hamiltonian.
assessment_summary:
1. [Justified] Assume for contradiction that a finite simple 3-regular, 3-connected graph G is not Hamiltonian.
2. [Justified] G contains a cycle: 3-connectivity implies minimum degree at least 3, and every finite graph of minimum degree at least 2 contains a cycle.
3. [Justified] Choose a longest cycle C. Since G is assumed non-Hamiltonian, G−V(C) has a nonempty connected component H.
4. [Justified] H has at least three distinct neighbors on C. Otherwise deleting its at most two neighbors on C would separate H from the remaining vertices of C, contrary to 3-connectivity.
5. [Not justified—the first failure] The attempted proof claims that among three neighbors of H on C, two must be consecutive on C. This is false: three vertices can be mutually separated around a sufficiently long cycle.
6. [Conditionally justified only] If consecutive vertices x,y of C were both adjacent to H, connectivity of H would give an x–y path whose internal vertices lie in H; replacing the edge xy by this path would produce a longer cycle. Step 5, however, does not establish the needed x,y.
7. [Not justified] The attempted contradiction with the maximality of C therefore does not follow, so this proof attempt cannot establish the statement.
8. [Justified] The statement is in fact false. Define P to have the ten 2-element subsets of {1,2,3,4,5} as vertices, with two vertices adjacent exactly when the subsets are disjoint.
9. [Justified] P is finite and simple, and every vertex has degree 3: a 2-subset is disjoint from exactly the three 2-subsets of its three-element complement.
10. [Justified] P is 3-connected. Permutations of {1,2,3,4,5} are automorphisms, and any pair of vertices is equivalent either to the adjacent pair 12,34 or to the nonadjacent pair 12,13. After deleting 12,34, the remaining vertices form the spanning path 25–13–45–23–14–35–24–15. After deleting 12,13, they form the spanning path 45–23–14–25–34–15–24–35. Thus deletion of any two vertices leaves P connected.
11. [Justified] Relabel P as outer vertices u0,…,u4 forming a 5-cycle, inner vertices v0,…,v4 with edges vi v(i+2), and spokes ui vi; one explicit relabeling is u=(12,34,15,23,45) and v=(35,25,24,14,13), with indices modulo 5.
12. [Justified] A Hamiltonian cycle would use a positive even number of spokes, hence either two or four. With two spokes, its restriction to each five-vertex layer would be a spanning path. The spoke indices would consequently have to differ by 1 modulo 5 in the outer cycle and by 2 modulo 5 in the inner cycle, which is impossible.
13. [Justified] With four spokes, suppose by cyclic symmetry that u0v0 is omitted. Degree two at every vertex forces the outer edges u4u0,u0u1,u2u3 and the inner edges v3v0,v0v2,v1v4. Together with the other four spokes, these form two disjoint 5-cycles, not one Hamiltonian cycle.
14. [Justified] Therefore P has no Hamiltonian cycle despite being 3-regular and 3-connected, so the asserted universal statement is false.
